newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Unofficial Papal poster criticised in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Unofficial Papal poster criticised in Sarajevo.

text.p: An unofficial poster announcing Pope John Paul's visit to Sarajevo this week has drawn sharp criticism from Moslem commentators for linking the religious leader to Croat nationalist symbols.
The placard shows young men and women waving flags with Croat symbols under a portrait of the Pope with the title, "He Comes to Us".
The poster was produced by the Catholic Youth Association without official authorisation from the organising committee for the April 12 visit, Roman Catholic church officials said.
The unofficial placard touched a raw nerve in a country devastated by a war among rival religious communities.
Bosnian Moslem newspapers condemned the poster as suggesting that the Pope was coming to Bosnia only for the sake of the Catholic Croat community.
The poster deserves "condemnation" as an attempt to manipulate an event which was important to Bosnians of all faiths, the daily Dnevni Avaz wrote on Friday.

The newspaper Oslobodjenje said the creators of the unofficial poster were promoting a self-styled Bosnian Croat mini-state which they call Herzeg-Bosna while revealing their ignorance of the Pope's support for Bosnian statehood and religious tolerance.
"Those who do not understand (the Pope's words, flutter the flags of Herzeg-Bosna," the newspaper said.
The official placard issued by the organising committee carries the title, "We Are With You" over a photograph of Pope John Paul II.
Vicar Mato Zovkic told Reuters the unofficial poster, which has been widely distributed in Croat-controlled areas in the western Herzegovina region, sent an inappropriate message.
The Pope was coming to Sarajevo to share in the suffering of all Bosnians during the 1992-95 war and to promote coexistence among Moslems, Orthodox Christian Serbs and Catholic Croats.
"Of course he's coming to see his fellow Catholics, but not exclusively, not primarily. He's coming primarily to Sarajevo to see all the inhabitants of this town," he said.
Zovkic, who serves under Bosnia's cardinal, said the unofficial poster presented a difficult problem. "I'm not happy about it...but I do understand their approach," he said.
Zovkic said a Croat priest in Mostar told him the poster was designed "to motivate Herzegovina Croats to come to Sarajevo because they don't like Sarajevo", he said.
"They say it is a Moslem city....They have to invent something like this to motivate Herzegovina Croats."
With a large membership in the western region, the church had to tolerate the poster as a way of encouraging Catholics to come to a city which now has a Moslem majority, he said.
"It's a very touchy question because we would like them to join us at the Pope's mass. We would like to have a full stadium and without Herzegovina people we cannot fill it."
During his first visit to Sarajevo next Saturday and Sunday, the Pope plans to hold mass in Kosevo soccer stadium.
Other church officials privately expressed concerns that recent tensions within the Moslem-Croat federation could discourage Croats from travelling to the Bosnian capital.
Catholic churches and monasteries have been the target of a wave of bombing attacks over the past couple months which have been condemned by Moslem and Croat political leaders.
Local elections in neighbouring Croatia, which are scheduled the same weekend as the Pope's visit, may also prevent many Catholics from making the trip to Bosnia.
